prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I wonder, by my troth, what thou and I Did, till we loved? Were we not weaned till then? But sucked on country pleasures, childishly? Or snorted we in the Seven Sleepers’ den? ’Twas so; but this, all pleasures fancies be. If ever any beauty I did see, Which I desired, and got, ’twas but a dream of thee. And now good-morrow to our waking souls, Which watch not one another out of fear; For love, all love of other sights controls, And makes one little room an everywhere. Let sea-discoverers to new worlds have gone, Let maps to other, worlds on worlds have shown, Let us possess one world, each hath one, and is one. My face in thine eye, thine in mine appears, And true plain hearts do in the faces rest; Where can we find two better hemispheres, Without sharp north, without declining west? Whatever dies, was not mixed equally; If our two loves be one, or, thou and I Love so alike, that none do slacken, none can die.

outputs.L2:
Honestly, I ask myself what you and I were doing before we fell in love. Had we not truly grown up until that moment? Were we merely feeding on simple, rustic pleasures like children? Or were we asleep, like the Seven Sleepers in their cave? Yes, that must have been the case; compared with this love, every earlier pleasure was only an illusion. If I ever saw any beauty before, desired it, and possessed it, it was only a shadow or dream of you.

And now, let us greet the morning of our awakened souls. They do not keep watch over each other out of suspicion or fear. Love governs and surpasses every attraction to anything else, and it can turn one small room into an entire universe. Let explorers sail away to discover new lands; let mapmakers chart world after world. We will hold our own world here: each of us contains a world, and together we are one.

My face is reflected in your eye, and yours is reflected in mine. Our honest, open hearts are visible in our faces. Where could anyone find two finer halves of a world than ours, with no harsh north and no fading west? Only things that are unevenly joined can perish. If our two loves are truly one, or if you and I love so equally that neither love weakens, then such love cannot die.
outputs.L3:
The speaker reflects on life before love as something immature, dreamlike, and incomplete. Everything that came before the beloved now seems childish, as if it belonged to a half-awake state rather than to true experience. Past pleasures, attractions, and beauties are dismissed as mere fantasies or shadows when compared with the reality of the beloved. What once seemed meaningful is now revealed to have been only a preparation for this deeper and more complete love.

Their love brings a powerful awakening. It rouses their souls into full awareness and frees them from fear, uncertainty, and the distractions of the outside world. In their shared intimacy, even a small room becomes large enough to contain an entire universe. Because they are wholly present to one another, they no longer need to seek fulfillment elsewhere; their private world feels complete in itself.

The lovers also see themselves reflected in each other, which suggests a profound mutual understanding. Each recognizes their own heart and truth in the other’s face, creating a sense of unity and perfect emotional balance. Their relationship is not one-sided or unstable, but equal, reciprocal, and harmonious.

The poem ultimately presents their love as so perfectly matched that it seems beyond decay. Because neither lover dominates the other and both give and receive in equal measure, their bond appears complete and enduring. This balanced love is imagined as something that cannot weaken or die, because it has achieved a rare state of spiritual and emotional perfection.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents love as a profound awakening, a moment in which the lovers move from an immature and incomplete past into a fuller, more meaningful present. At the beginning, the speaker looks back on the time before their love and describes it as a period of childish pleasures, dreams, and half-conscious experience. Whatever they enjoyed before seems insignificant now, as though their earlier lives were only a kind of sleep. True love has transformed their understanding of themselves and of the world.

This transformation is expressed through images of discovery and exploration. The poem refers to “sea-discoverers” and “new worlds,” suggesting the excitement of geographical conquest and the expansion of human knowledge. However, the speaker implies that the lovers’ private world is greater than any physical discovery. They do not need to travel outward in search of new lands, because they have found an entire world in one another. Their room becomes a complete universe, made meaningful by their shared devotion.

The poem also emphasizes the equality and reciprocity of their love. The lovers look into each other’s eyes and see their own faces reflected there, suggesting a perfect mutual recognition. Neither lover dominates the other; instead, each gives and receives love in equal measure. This balance makes their relationship harmonious and self-sufficient. Their love is not based on illusion, possession, or imbalance, but on a deep unity between two people who fully acknowledge one another.

By the end of the poem, this mutual love is presented as something beyond decay. The speaker suggests that because their love is equal and complete, it cannot weaken or die. Unlike worldly achievements, which are temporary and often incomplete, the lovers’ union forms a stable and “deathless” world of its own. The poem therefore celebrates true love as an awakening into a richer reality, one in which two people become each other’s whole world and find in their shared affection something more valuable than any external conquest or discovery.
outputs.L5:
**Did, Were, But**

Did you ever wonder why some days feel easy and others feel difficult? There were moments when everything seemed clear, but there were also times when challenges appeared without warning. What matters most is not whether the day was perfect, but how we responded to it.

People did their best, even when they were tired or unsure. They made mistakes, but they also learned from them. They were not always successful, but they kept trying. In the end, progress did not come from being perfect; it came from being patient, brave, and willing to continue.

Life is full of “did,” “were,” and “but” moments: what we did, who we were, and what stood in our way. But every obstacle can become a lesson, and every lesson can help us grow.

**The Good-Morrow**  
by John Donne

I wonder, by my troth, what thou and I  
Did, till we loved? were we not weaned till then?  
But sucked on country pleasures, childishly?  
Or snorted we in the Seven Sleepers’ den?  
’Twas so; but this, all pleasures fancies be.  
If ever any beauty I did see,  
Which I desired, and got, ’twas but a dream of thee.

And now good-morrow to our waking souls,  
Which watch not one another out of fear;  
For love, all love of other sights controls,  
And makes one little room an everywhere.  
Let sea-discoverers to new worlds have gone,  
Let maps to others, worlds on worlds have shown,  
Let us possess one world, each hath one, and is one.

My face in thine eye, thine in mine appears,  
And true plain hearts do in the faces rest;  
Where can we find two better hemispheres,  
Without sharp north, without declining west?  
Whatever dies, was not mixed equally;  
If our two loves be one, or, thou and I  
Love so alike, that none do slacken, none can die.
